title: The Queen's Gambit
subtitle: The gambit that isn't — and how to punish greed.
goals: Understand why c4 is not a real pawn sacrifice
Know the difference between accepting and declining
Punish an attempt to hold the extra pawn

steps.say: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 — the Queen's Gambit, the most respected opening move order in classical chess. It's called a gambit, but it isn't one: Black can take the pawn on c4, and White will always win it back. What White is really offering is a wing pawn for control of the centre.
Declining is the main line. 2...e6 is the Queen's Gambit Declined: solid, slightly passive, and played in more World Championship games than any other opening.

autoMoves.say: 2...e6, declining. Black keeps a pawn on d5 and accepts a slightly boxed-in light bishop.
4.Bg5, pinning the knight that defends d5 — the same indirect pressure idea as the Ruy Lopez.
Black unpins by hand. This is the classical QGD, and White's edge is small but permanent.

steps.say: Accepting is fine too — 2...dxc4 3.e3, and White simply plays Bxc4 next move. What is NOT fine is trying to keep the pawn. Black has just played 3...b5??, propping up c4 with a pawn. It looks like a fortress. You're White; it's a house of cards.

steps.prompt: Black is trying to hold the gambit pawn with 3...b5. Blow the queenside open and win material — in three moves.
hints: Undermine the pawn that's doing the propping. Which of your pawns can attack b5?
a4! Black defends with c6, but then you exchange twice on b5 and open the long diagonal.
a4 c6 axb5 cxb5 and now the a8 rook is naked — find the queen move that hits it.

line.say: Attacking the base of Black's little pawn chain. Black's most natural defence is to add another pawn...
Opening the a-file and forcing matters. Black has to recapture, and doing so with the c-pawn empties the long diagonal completely.

And there it is. The a8-h1 diagonal has no pawn left on it — b7 went to b5, c6 was traded — so your queen attacks the rook on a8 from f3. Black cannot defend it adequately, and the greedy attempt to keep one pawn has cost the exchange.

rejections.say: Attacking c4 from the other side is met by ...cxb3 and Black's queenside pawns survive. The pawn to attack is b5, the one holding the whole structure together — and the pawn that attacks it is on a2.
You can't — and if you could, bxc4 just wins a piece. Undermine the defender first: a4.
A fine central move that ignores the queenside entirely. Black consolidates with ...Bb7 and ...e6 and really is a pawn up. Punish the structure while it's still loose: a4.
Developing is almost never wrong, but here it hands Black a free tempo to play ...Bb7 and ...e6 and genuinely keep the pawn. The refutation is a pawn move, and it's available right now.

steps.wrongSay: Black's c4 pawn is held up by b5. Which white pawn can attack b5 — and what happens to the long diagonal after the trades?
steps.successSay: That's why the Queen's Gambit isn't a gambit: take the pawn if you like, but try to KEEP it and the whole queenside falls apart.
